text: Sooner or later you will train a model and the loss will simply not go down. The temptation is to start turning knobs at random, a different learning rate here, another layer there, but a neural network with a bug rarely crashes; it just quietly learns badly. A short, ordered checklist finds most problems far faster than guessing, so let us walk through one.

Start with the data, because it is the most common culprit. Print a few examples together with their labels and check that they really match; a classic bug shuffles the inputs and the labels separately, so every example is paired with someone else's answer. Check the shapes at each stage and the range of the values, since raw pixel values up to two hundred and fifty-five behave very differently from features scaled near zero.

Next, check the very first loss: for a classifier it should be close to the log of the number of classes. Then try the most useful test of all. Take one tiny batch, a handful of examples, and train on it alone. A working model can memorise a handful of examples almost perfectly, so the loss should fall nearly to zero. If it cannot, the problem is in your code, not in your data or your model size.

If you wrote the gradients yourself, check them numerically. Nudge one weight up by a tiny amount h, then down by h, measure the loss both times, and divide the difference by two h. That finite difference approximates the slope, and it should agree closely with your analytic gradient. A large disagreement points straight at the layer with the mistake.

Then watch the training itself. If the loss becomes not a number, look for a learning rate that is too high, a log of zero, or a division by zero. Print the size of the gradients in each layer: gradients that are vanishingly small mean the early layers have stopped learning, while huge ones mean the steps are exploding. And check the activations, since a layer whose ReLU units all output zero has gone dead and passes nothing on.

Some bugs are almost silent. A broadcasting mismatch between shapes B by one and B turns a loss into the wrong number without any error. Forgetting to clear old gradients, or adding the gradient instead of subtracting it, quietly sabotages every update. And a classic in PyTorch: its cross-entropy loss expects raw logits, so applying softmax yourself before calling it squashes the signal and slows learning.

The same discipline scales up. Teams training language models run small versions first, check that tiny runs behave as expected, and only then spend real compute, because a silent bug at full scale can waste weeks. That completes training in practice. Next, we begin convolutional networks, with convolution as a sliding pattern detector.
